answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Top-level resource type (account): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (API-specific child resources: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and /mongoCollections in some ARM versions).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example to create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create --name myDocDbAccount --resource-group myRg --locations regionName=eastus --kind MongoDB

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (e.g. resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' ... } ). Terraform resource: azurerm_cosmosdb_account (provider azurerm) with kind = "MongoDB" and appropriate capabilities/settings.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Use a Mongo URI (SRV or standard). SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Non-SRV form: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Port (non-SRV) is 10255 and SSL must be enabled (ssl=true). retryWrites is typically false for Cosmos Mongo compatibility.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is managed at the Cosmos DB account level. Typical Cosmos models are provisioned throughput measured in Request Units/sec (RUs) and autoscale RUs; there is also a serverless option for some accounts. Some managed Mongo offerings expose instance/compute tiers (M-series/vCores) in addition to RU-based billing, but the mainstream Azure model is provisioned RUs (or serverless).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary authentication for the Mongo API is username/password (Mongo users created on the account; SCRAM). Cosmos/Mongo accounts also expose primary keys for SQL API; Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) authentication is available for some Cosmos APIs but is not the default for the Mongo wire protocol. If Azure AD were supported for Mongo, the driver would use an access token obtained from Entra ID and pass it as the password or via SASL/OAUTHBEARER mechanism, but in practice use username/password (SCRAM) for drivers.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the official MongoDB drivers for your language (for Python, use pymongo). Do not use the Azure Cosmos SDK for Mongo-programmed workloads; the Mongo wire protocol is served so use mongodb-compatible client libraries.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Vector/index types exposed on Mongo-compatible Azure DocumentDB variants are not the same as native MongoDB indexes; recent managed clusters advertise HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. A plausible create-index call (Mongo shell-like) is: db.myCollection.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536, distance: 'cosine' }). Note: exact option names (algorithm, dims, distance) depend on the service extension; this is the form I'd attempt first.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text/hybrid search is typically provided by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search (Azure Search) for Cosmos DB. For Mongo-like vector+text hybrid search you either use the provider's built-in vector index + text index if available, or combine a text index (Azure Search or service-specific search extension) with the vector index in the application to do hybrid ranking.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Managed Azure Mongo-compatible accounts advertise a supported MongoDB server wire protocol version (commonly 4.2/5.0/6.0/7.0 depending on account). Expect most core CRUD and aggregation pipeline features to work, but some server-side features (server-side JS, all admin commands, certain change-stream/transaction semantics, or unsupported aggregation stages) may be missing or limited. Verify the exact supported server version on the account.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full-featured local emulator for the Mongo-compatible Azure service. For local development run the official MongoDB Docker image (example: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:7) and connect on port 27017. For testing against the real service use the cluster in DOCUMENTDB_URI.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Support for MongoDB change streams depends on the managed Mongo compatibility and server version; some Cosmos Mongo-compatible accounts support watch()/change streams for supported versions, while others do not. If supported, nothing special beyond using a driver that calls collection.watch() is required; otherwise change streams are not available. I would assume change streams may be unavailable on some SKUs and set low confidence.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the service-specific MCP server named documentdb (mcp server 'documentdb'). The general Azure MCP server does not provide the Mongo-specific inspection tools; the 'documentdb' MCP server provides collection/index inspection and query-plan tooling for this service.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's proprietary JSON document database service; it has since been rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. "Azure DocumentDB" as a name historically refers to the same Microsoft managed service lineage; it is distinct from any open-source project named DocumentDB. Cosmos DB hosts several APIs (SQL/Core, MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table) that surface different wire protocols.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the Mongo-compatible API the service exposes the MongoDB wire protocol but the storage/engine is the provider's proprietary engine (Cosmos engine) with Mongo compatibility. For application code, use standard MongoDB drivers and expect most code to work, but watch for provider-specific limitations, slight differences in supported commands, throughput semantics, and indexing/aggregation edge-cases.

answers.question: What database name should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use database name sample_customer_360_03 for all collections created and queries the sample runs.

answers.question: Which Python client and connection pattern will the sample use?
answers.answer: Use pymongo. Read the Mongo connection URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to pymongo.MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']) (support both mongodb+srv and mongodb schemes).

answers.question: What collection names and a candidate vector index definition will the sample create?
answers.answer: Collections: propensity, preferences, timing, nba_recommendations. Candidate vector index creation (mongo shell-like attempt): db.propensity.createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}, {algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536, distance: 'cosine'}). If that command fails, fall back to creating a standard sparse index on an embedding field and use client-side nearest-neighbor search.

answers.question: Which port should the sample try if the DOCUMENTDB_URI is not SRV and does not include a port?
answers.answer: Assume the non-SRV TLS Mongo port 10255 (e.g. <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255) and require ssl=true in the URI.

answers.question: What MCP tool/command will be used to inspect collections, indexes and query plans during the build?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server tools (connection profile 'default') — for example mcp documentdb list-collections --db sample_customer_360_03 and mcp documentdb show-indexes --collection propensity to inspect indexes and verify creations.
